extracted.intended_audience: aspiring TV comedy writers and writers-room participants (people who want to punch up sitcom scripts or break into TV comedy)
extracted.subtask_description: A workshop-style curriculum for crafting effective jokes specifically for television sitcoms and for participating productively in a TV writers' room/punch-up session. Covers joke mechanics, types of TV jokes, scene construction, writers' room terminology, and practical punch-up practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Medium-specific suitability
rubrics_metrics.description: Jokes don’t just come out of nowhere, and their success is completely reliant on the medium. Things that are funny in conversation or in front of an audience might not be funny on a television show.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether a joke fits television as a medium (timing, visual beats, delivery constraints) rather than just being 'naturally funny' in other contexts. Tailor jokes to what works on-screen and within an episode structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Where Do the Best Jokes Come From?
rubrics_metrics.description: Learn the art of TV joke writing by understanding where good jokes come from and the elements needed to make a joke work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explore sources and processes for finding jokes in a script (character-driven, situation-driven, callbacks, etc.). Recognize that many great jokes emerge through group ideation in a punch-up room rather than in isolation.

rubrics_metrics.name: What Makes a Great TV Joke?
rubrics_metrics.description: Break down what makes a joke work on television and the elements needed to make a joke work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider structural and tonal elements (see specific sub-elements below such as logical surprise, word count, sounds, rule of three, and appropriate use of puns). A great TV joke aligns with scene objectives and character POV.

rubrics_metrics.name: The logical surprise
rubrics_metrics.description: The logical surprise (listed as a core element of what makes a great TV joke).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create a punchline that surprises but remains logically connected to the setup — the surprise must make sense within the scene and characters' reality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thinking about number of words
rubrics_metrics.description: Thinking about number of words (as an element of effective TV jokes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be concise: optimize word count for timing and delivery. Shorter beats often land better on TV; evaluate rhythm and how many words a performer must deliver.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sounds of words
rubrics_metrics.description: Sounds of words (consideration for joke construction).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose words for their sonic qualities — alliteration, rhythm, and cadence can enhance comedic impact. Test lines aloud to hear how sound shapes the joke.

rubrics_metrics.name: The rule of 3
rubrics_metrics.description: The rule of 3 (a fundamental comedic device listed in the curriculum).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use set-up/set-up/punch or pattern-plus-surprise structures. Evaluate whether listing or grouping items benefits from the comedic payoff of a third element that subverts expectation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Puns — yes or no?
rubrics_metrics.description: Puns — yes or no? (explicitly listed as a topic to consider when writing TV jokes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge when puns serve the character/scene versus when they feel cheap or distracting. Consider tone of show and audience tolerance for wordplay before using puns.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Main Types of TV Jokes
rubrics_metrics.description: An overview of the main types of TV jokes you can draw from.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Learn categories (e.g., gag, callback, visual joke, one-liner, running gag, character-based humor) and choose types that fit show tone and scene objectives. Use type-appropriate setup and timing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Familiarity with writers-room joke terminology
rubrics_metrics.description: Other Important Joke Terminology: Alts, Blow, Pipe, House Number, Side Trips, Callbacks, Button, Runners, Hard Joke, A side/B side.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Know and use standard punch-up vocabulary so you can participate effectively in rooms. Understand what 'alt' or 'button' means in practice and how to craft each.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scene construction (POV, objective, change agent)
rubrics_metrics.description: Scene Construction — What is the POV? What is being accomplished? Who is changing the course of the scene?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate scenes for point-of-view, clear objectives, and which character shifts the scene; craft jokes that serve the scene's purpose and character beats rather than existing as standalone gags.

rubrics_metrics.name: What is a punch up and why is it important?
rubrics_metrics.description: What is a punch up and why is it so important? (topic covered to explain the role and value of punch-up work).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand punch-ups as the collaborative process of making existing scenes funnier — important for preparing pilots and for being a valuable room member. Use punch-ups to enhance character, rhythm, and episode flow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elements of a TV punch up room
rubrics_metrics.description: Elements of a TV punch up room (listed as a learning item).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Learn the structural elements of punch-up sessions (roles, document workflows like alt docs, how pitches are offered and recorded, etiquette) so you can contribute efficiently and professionally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategies to be successful and serve as an asset in a punch up room
rubrics_metrics.description: Strategies to be successful and serve as an asset in a punch up room (explicit learning objective).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt practical tactics: pitch quickly and clearly, offer alts, listen and build on others' ideas, avoid derailing the room with half-baked jokes, and understand note-taking/alt-doc conventions to be helpful rather than disruptive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punch-up practical skills: add jokes, fill in pitches, create alt docs
rubrics_metrics.description: In the workshop participants will 'add jokes, fill in pitches, and create alt docs' for scenes in a group setting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practice concrete deliverables: produce alternate lines (alts), write concise pitch phrasing, and prepare 'alt docs' that show multiple options. Expect instructor feedback on joke pitches and finished alts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collaborative dynamics and common room pitfalls
rubrics_metrics.description: Workshop addresses real-room obstacles such as pitching half-baked ideas or getting stuck on a single concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Learn to recognize and avoid anti-patterns (e.g., over-investing in one joke, failing to move on, not building on teammates' contributions). Instructor feedback focuses on overcoming these common problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scene-to-joke fit (serve scene objectives)
rubrics_metrics.description: Make jokes work with an eye towards scene construction and explain what makes a great punch up room for any TV comedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always evaluate whether a joke serves the scene's POV, advances action/character, or simply distracts. Prioritize jokes that accomplish a scene's goal or reveal character.
